Phobos. The larger of Mars's two moons, orbiting much closer to the planet than any other known moon in the solar system. It was discovered in eighteen seventy-seven by American astronomer Asaph Hall and is named after the Greek god of fear. Phobos is slowly spiraling toward Mars and will eventually be torn apart by tidal forces.

Phobos is only about twenty-two kilometers across, making it extremely small—smaller than the asteroid Apophis. It orbits Mars every seven point six six hours, faster than Mars rotates. From the Martian surface, Phobos rises in the west and sets in the east, an unusual sight. The moon is heavily cratered and has an irregular potato shape. Its largest crater, Stickney, is ten kilometers across.

Phobos is synchronously tidally locked, always showing the same face to Mars. The density of the moon suggests it originated as a captured asteroid rather than co-accreting with Mars in the early solar system. In roughly thirty to fifty million years, Mars's gravity will shred Phobos into a ring system that will orbit the planet. Asaph Hall used the U.S. Naval Observatory telescope to discover both of Mars's moons, naming them after the Greek gods of panic and dread.
